title: Opinion and discursive writing
summary: Answer a position-based prompt with a defensible qualified claim, developed reasons, evidence-bounded examples and a fair response to relevant complexity when that prompt family is offered.

sections.title: Answer the position task that is actually offered
content: Use an opinion or discursive response only when the prompt asks for a position, evaluation or discussion. The available public evidence does not establish that every reported test sitting offers this prompt family. Read the command precisely: ‘Do you agree?’ requires a clear answer, while ‘Discuss’ may require a broader comparison before a reasoned judgement.

Opinion writing does not mean unsupported preference, and discursive writing does not mean giving equal space to every imaginable view. Both forms require a controlling answer that the reasons can defend. Before planning, complete: ‘My answer is … because …, although …’. This exposes the position, main basis and relevant limit.

sections.title: Make the position precise enough to defend
content: A defensible position states what should happen, under which important conditions and why. ‘Community service is good’ is too broad. ‘Schools should expect one service contribution each term, provided students can choose from accessible roles and use a genuine hardship alternative’ identifies the proposal and prevents the argument from depending on one identical arrangement for everyone.

Qualification is not indecision when it defines the conditions that make the position reasonable. Avoid absolute claims such as ‘every student will become caring’ or ‘this policy can never create pressure’. A narrower claim can be developed honestly from the available record.

sections.title: Develop each reason through a complete chain
content: Build a paragraph through claim, relevant detail, explanation and significance. Claim: a structured term commitment can make participation more dependable than an unplanned invitation. Detail from a fictional school record: the reading-support coordinator cannot prepare pairs when volunteers leave without notice. Explanation: choosing a defined role and schedule makes the expected contribution visible. Significance: the proposal answers a practical weakness in the optional arrangement without proving that every compulsory programme works.

An example does not explain itself. After each detail, ask what it shows, how it supports the reason and where its limits are. Do not turn one coordinator's concern into a universal statistic or claim that the policy will solve every community need.

sections.title: Represent the strongest relevant objection fairly
content: A useful counterargument could change the design or strength of the position. Students with long journeys, caregiving duties or limited transport may be unfairly burdened by a weekend-only external project. This is stronger than a weak objection such as ‘some students dislike helping’, because it identifies an access problem the proposal must answer.

State the objection in language a reasonable critic could accept. Avoid straw-man phrases such as ‘Opponents do not care about the community’. Fair representation improves the writer's own reasoning by testing the position against a real constraint.

sections.title: Concede what is valid, then respond
content: Use a concession-response chain: acknowledge the valid concern, explain its effect on the proposal, then show what position remains defensible. ‘A fixed weekend project could exclude students with travel or family responsibilities; therefore, a fair requirement would need supervised on-campus roles, a choice of times and a genuine equivalent or exemption. With those protections, expecting one bounded contribution can still be reasonable.’

The response changes the design rather than pretending the objection disappears. Do not use ‘however’ to repeat the original claim without answering the concern, and do not abandon the whole position merely because it needs conditions.

sections.title: Keep the route reasoned rather than repetitive
content: A focused route can use five jobs: answer and qualify the prompt; develop the first reason; develop a distinct second reason; address the strongest relevant objection; conclude with the judgement and its conditions. The conclusion should synthesise what has been established, not introduce a new reason or promise a perfect outcome.

Reverse-outline each paragraph with its claim and job. Repair assertion stacks by adding explanation, unsupported certainty by narrowing the claim, example dumps by linking each detail, false balance by making a judgement, and straw-man objections by stating the real constraint fairly.

sections.title: Plan one qualified position response
content: Use an original fictional school-service policy record. Make six decisions about task fit, the controlling position, relevant support, developed reasoning, fair counterargument and concession-response structure before viewing feedback.
